```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
has_igraph <- requireNamespace("igraph", quietly = TRUE)
has_network <- requireNamespace("network", quietly = TRUE)
```

knappnet works on networks stored as two data frames, one for nodes and one
for edges. Every measure returns a vector (or a data frame) aligned with the
rows of the node table, so results become ordinary columns that you can
summarize, plot, or model with the tools you already use.

This vignette covers the essentials: building a network, computing
measures, weights, conversion to and from other packages, and files. If
you already use another tool, the guides on the website map its functions
to knappnet's:
[igraph](https://knapply.github.io/knappnet/articles/coming-from-igraph.html),
[statnet and sna](https://knapply.github.io/knappnet/articles/coming-from-statnet.html),
[UCINET, ORA, Pajek, and Gephi](https://knapply.github.io/knappnet/articles/coming-from-ucinet-ora-pajek-gephi.html),
and [NetworkX](https://knapply.github.io/knappnet/articles/coming-from-networkx.html).

```{r}
library(knappnet)
```

## Networks are two data frames

Padgett's data on marriages among leading families of Renaissance Florence
(Breiger and Pattison 1986) is a classic first network. Each row of `ties`
is a marriage tie between two families:

```{r}
ties <- data.frame(
  source = c("Acciaiuoli", "Medici", "Medici", "Medici", "Medici", "Medici",
           "Castellani", "Castellani", "Castellani", "Peruzzi", "Peruzzi",
           "Strozzi", "Strozzi", "Ridolfi", "Tornabuoni", "Albizzi", "Albizzi",
           "Salviati", "Bischeri", "Guadagni"),
  target   = c("Medici", "Barbadori", "Ridolfi", "Tornabuoni", "Albizzi", "Salviati",
           "Peruzzi", "Strozzi", "Barbadori", "Strozzi", "Bischeri",
           "Ridolfi", "Bischeri", "Tornabuoni", "Guadagni", "Ginori", "Guadagni",
           "Pazzi", "Guadagni", "Lamberteschi")
)
```

The Pucci family married outside this group, so it appears in no tie. A
node table keeps it in the network as an isolate, and holds any node
attributes:

```{r}
families <- data.frame(name = sort(unique(c(ties$source, ties$target, "Pucci"))))
flo <- net_frame(ties, nodes = families, directed = FALSE, id = "name")
flo
```

The printed card says what kind of network this is (undirected, one mode,
unweighted, static, simple) and previews both tables. The endpoint
columns are named by `source` and `target`, whose defaults are the column
names `"source"` and `"target"`, and the identifier column by `id`
(default `"id"`); column names and positions are never guessed. Without
`nodes`, the node table is built from the edge list, in order of first
appearance, and isolates are necessarily missing. Any other columns are
attributes and are carried along untouched.

The tables are checked before anything is computed, and every problem is
reported at once, with the rows concerned:

```{r, error = TRUE}
bad <- data.frame(source = c("Medici", NA, "Strozzi"), target = c("Pazzi", "Ginori", "Medcii"))
net_frame(bad, nodes = families, directed = FALSE, id = "name")
```

`plot()` draws a network with no further arguments:

```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 5}
plot(flo, seed = 1)
```

The two tables are plain data frames:

```{r}
head(flo$nodes)
head(flo$edges)
```

## Measures

Each node-level measure returns one value per row of `flo$nodes`, in the
same order, so results can be stored directly as columns:

```{r}
flo$nodes$degree <- net_degree(flo)
flo$nodes$betweenness <- net_betweenness(flo)
flo$nodes$harmonic <- round(net_harmonic(flo, normalized = TRUE), 3)
flo$nodes$core <- net_coreness(flo)
flo$nodes[order(-flo$nodes$betweenness), ]
```

Results stored as columns can be drawn directly:

```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 5}
plot(flo, node_size = "betweenness", node_color = "core", seed = 1)
```

The Medici lie on far more shortest paths between other families than
anyone else, in line with Padgett and Ansell's (1993) account of the
family's rise, which stresses its ties to families that were not tied to
one another.

Harmonic centrality is shown here instead of closeness because the Pucci
cannot reach anyone. Closeness sums distances to the other nodes, and
programs disagree about what to do with distances that do not exist:

```{r}
net_closeness(flo)[flo$nodes$name == "Pucci"]
```

Under [igraph](https://r.igraph.org/)'s convention, the default, a node that reaches no one gets
`NaN`. The `convention` argument reproduces the choices of [NetworkX](https://networkx.org/), [sna](https://cran.r-project.org/package=sna),
or [UCINET](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/home) instead; `?conventions` and the
[conventions guide](https://knapply.github.io/knappnet/articles/conventions.html)
explain every difference.

Measures of the whole network return a single number, or a list:

```{r}
net_density(flo)
net_centralization(flo, "degree")
comp <- net_components(flo)
comp$no
comp$csize
```

Groups of nodes are returned as membership vectors aligned with the nodes,
or as lists of node identifiers:

```{r}
net_max_cliques(flo, min_size = 3)
groups <- net_louvain(flo, seed = 1)
table(groups)
```

Louvain community detection visits nodes in a random order, so it takes a
seed; the same seed gives the same result on any computer and with any
number of threads. Without one, a seed is drawn from R's generator, so
`set.seed()` works as usual.

## Weighted networks

A network without a weight column is binary, and every algorithm uses its
fastest unweighted form. With weights, you say once what they mean.
Distances (travel time, cost, latency) keep nodes apart:

```{r}
roads <- data.frame(
  source    = c("a", "b", "a"),
  target      = c("b", "c", "c"),
  minutes = c(5, 5, 20)
)
trips <- net_frame(roads, directed = FALSE, weight = "minutes", weight_type = "distance")
trips
net_betweenness(trips)                    # a to c is quicker through b
net_betweenness(trips, weighted = FALSE)  # ignoring travel time
```

Strengths (contact frequency, tie intensity) bring nodes closer, so
path-based measures use 1/weight as the length, while measures that add up
weights use them as given:

```{r}
calls <- data.frame(
  source  = c("a", "b", "a"),
  target    = c("b", "c", "c"),
  calls = c(1, 1, 20)
)
phone <- net_frame(calls, directed = FALSE, weight = "calls", weight_type = "strength")
net_betweenness(phone)  # a and c talk directly, so b brokers nothing
net_strength(phone)
```

The same three edges, read as distances and as strengths, give different
shortest paths from `a` to `c`; edges are drawn wider the stronger they
are, and distances do not change the width:

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
xy <- plot(trips, main = "minutes (distance)", edge_color = I(c("black", "black", "gray")),
           seed = 2)
plot(phone, layout = xy, main = "calls (strength)",
     edge_color = I(c("gray", "gray", "black")))
par(op)
```

Path-based measures take `weighted` (use the weights or not) and
`weights_as` (read them as `"distance"` or `"strength"` for this call
only). Measures defined only on binary ties, such as cliques, the triad
census, and brokerage, ignore weights and say so in their help pages.

## Kinds of networks

The same two tables hold every kind of network; roles name the columns
that carry structure. Two-mode data take a `mode` column (or
`net_twomode()`), multiplex data a `relation` column, signed data a `sign`
column, temporal data `start` (and `end`) or `wave` columns, spatial data
coordinate columns or sf geometry, multilayer data the layers of each
endpoint, egocentric data an `ego` column, and unobserved pairs or
non-respondents logical flags. The card and the plot show each of them:

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.5}
women <- net_example("southern_women")
women
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(women, node_label = FALSE, main = "two-mode: women and events")
plot(net_example("krackhardt"), node_label = FALSE, main = "multiplex: three relations",
     seed = 1)
par(op)
```

The [network types](https://knapply.github.io/knappnet/articles/network-types.html)
article shows every configuration with its tables, card, and plot, and the
[definitions](https://knapply.github.io/knappnet/articles/definitions.html)
article explains the choices behind them.

## Conversion

`as.matrix()` gives the adjacency matrix, and `as_net_frame()` turns a
matrix back into a network. Direction is inferred from symmetry, and
values other than 0 and 1 become weights:

```{r}
m <- matrix(c(0, 2, 0,
              2, 0, 1,
              0, 1, 0), 3, byrow = TRUE,
            dimnames = list(c("x", "y", "z"), c("x", "y", "z")))
small <- as_net_frame(m)
small
small$edges
as.matrix(small, attr = "weight")
```

Networks also convert both ways with [igraph](https://r.igraph.org/), [tidygraph](https://tidygraph.data-imaginist.com/), and [statnet](https://statnet.org/)'s
network package, keeping node, edge, and network attributes:

```{r, eval = has_igraph}
ig <- net_to_igraph(flo)
igraph::vcount(ig)
head(igraph::vertex_attr(ig, "betweenness"))
karate <- as_net_frame(igraph::make_graph("Zachary"))
karate
```

```{r, eval = has_network}
net <- net_to_network(flo)
network::network.size(net)
```

`net_to_tbl_graph()` returns a tidygraph object, and the usual generics of
those packages, `igraph::as.igraph()`, `network::as.network()`, and
`tidygraph::as_tbl_graph()`, also accept a net_frame.

## Files

`net_read()` and `net_write()` handle GraphML, GEXF, GML, [Pajek](http://mrvar.fdv.uni-lj.si/pajek/),
[UCINET](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/home) DL, JSON node-link, [ORA](https://www.casos.cs.cmu.edu/projects/ora/)'s DyNetML, CSV and TSV edge lists, and
(write only) DOT. The format comes from the file extension:

```{r}
path <- tempfile(fileext = ".graphml")
net_write(flo, path)
back <- net_read(path)
back
head(back$nodes)
```

GraphML records attribute types, so the computed columns come back as they
were. An edge list cannot record isolates or node attributes, so a CSV
edge list is written with an optional node file alongside it:

```{r}
edges_csv <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
nodes_csv <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
net_write(flo, edges_csv, nodes_file = nodes_csv)
net_read(edges_csv, nodes = nodes_csv, directed = FALSE)
```
